idiom_name: pending-request hash (uthash macros or a hand-rolled bucket list) + pthread_cond_timedwait
implementation_notes: C has no awaitable, so the requestor hand-builds all three parts: a request struct (id, mutex, condition variable, done flag, reply storage, absolute deadline), a hash table keyed by the id - uthash's HASH_ADD_INT / HASH_FIND_INT / HASH_DEL, or a hand-rolled bucket list - guarded by a table mutex, and a reader thread that extracts the correlation id from each reply, removes the entry and signals the condition variable. The caller waits with pthread_cond_timedwait against an absolute deadline and re-checks its predicate in a loop because condition waits wake spuriously, treating ETIMEDOUT as the no-reply outcome. Nothing replaces the structure in C; the parts to get right are the hand-off order (add to the table before sending) and ownership of the request struct after a timeout, since the table and the waiter must agree on who frees it.
pitfalls: pthread_cond_timedwait takes an ABSOLUTE time (clock_gettime plus seconds), not a relative delay, and may return 0 spuriously - always re-check the done predicate in a while loop and use the same clock for both.
A fast reply can arrive before the entry is in the hash table: register the request before publishing it, otherwise the reader finds no entry and drops the reply.

The reader must remove the entry and signal while holding the table mutex, and the timeout path must agree with it on who frees the request struct; touching it after the caller timed out and freed it is a use-after-free.
ETIMEDOUT does not prove the predicate is false - the reply may have arrived at the same instant - so re-check under the mutex before reporting a timeout.
